newsitem.title: UK: Coffee--Physicals stay quiet as buyers avoid May.
newsitem.headline: Coffee--Physicals stay quiet as buyers avoid May.

text.p: Physical coffee markets stayed quiet this week as European demand slowed for the higher-priced May coffee while enquiries for second half 1997 arabicas met with few sellers.
Traders said stabilising futures prices since Monday after weeks of volatility gave the market a long overdue breather but fresh deals were still hard to come by.
"It's easier to do business as the market is less volatile. It gives us a more breathing space," said one.
New York and London futures markets ambled in a narrow range since Monday after falling late last week on fund long liquidation.
While the fund shake-out in coffee appeared to have ended for now, traders said the market was still vulnerable to sharp moves especially in the medium-term due to the approaching Brazilian winter.

The last major frosts in mid-1994 damaged the Brazilian crop and sent futures prices sky-rocketing. World coffee prices had risen by more than 50 percent this year on forecasts of a lower Brazilian crop and supply disruptions in Colombia.
In physicals, traders noted a reasonable interest in prompt robustas to fill in cover for the Western hemisphere summer months.
In arabicas, there were enquiries for Brazilian material up to September shipments but business was slow as producers returned from the long Easter holidays.
Arabica stocks have increased sharply in Europe after the heavy purchases in January and February during the blistering rally.
"There have been further offers from all origins against the premium May and almost no offers for shipments from May onwards," said one European trader.

New York's May arabica futures has been holding at a large 13-18 cents a lb premium over second-position July, prompting sellers already heavily sold against March to offer additional quantities in May.
There is still a fair interest in May or June shipments but the volume has shrank sharply as buyers awaited lower prices against the July contracts in London or New York.
"Most dealers want to sell spot/float priced against May but roasters want May/June shipments against July and July/August against September," another said.
In robustas, traders reported steady arrivals from Cameroon, Ivory Coast and Zaire but the supply situation in Uganda was a bit tight with the main crop tailing off.
There were still cheap offers for Vietnam and Indonesian beans mainly from Singapore dealers.
